title: Europe's Ancient Forests Were Open and Sunny
summary:
Picture Europe a long, long time ago. You might imagine a dark forest of tall trees stretching as far as you can see. But scientists say that picture is probably wrong.

Instead, much of Europe was open and sunny, with scattered trees, grassy clearings, and meadows full of wildflowers. Birds and butterflies lived in these bright places, and huge plant-eating animals kept the trees and bushes from taking over.

Researchers led by Aarhus University found that this mix of open land and woodland was the normal landscape for more than 20 million years. The thick, dark forests we see in many places today came much later.

The study was published in the journal Biological Conservation. It raises questions about tree-planting programs today, which often plant dense forests to fight climate change and protect wildlife.

Professor Jens-Christian Svenning of Aarhus University, who led the study, says planting only dense forests could harm wildlife, because Europe's animals and plants grew up in open landscapes over millions of years.
why_it_matters: The parks and green spaces near your home are shaped by the same choices about trees and open land, and getting the mix right helps birds and butterflies thrive.

background_read: A long time ago, much of Europe was not covered in thick, dark forest, but was a mix of open sunny land and patches of trees.
Big plant-eating animals helped keep the land open by eating trees and bushes, so birds and butterflies had bright places to live.
Today, people often plant dense forests to fight climate change, but that may not suit the animals and plants that grew up in open landscapes.
